name: Cicalfate+

card.summary: Cicalfate+ is a French pharmacy repair cream from Avene, built around sucralfate and copper-zinc salts, used to calm and help irritated, damaged skin look better.
card.note: Studies are small and mostly in radiation dermatitis.

quick.overview:
Cicalfate+ is a restorative cream from the French brand Avene. It contains sucralfate, a compound otherwise known as an oral ulcer drug, together with copper and zinc salts. People use it on irritated or damaged skin, for example after cosmetic procedures, to calm the look of the skin.

In one small open French trial of women having breast radiotherapy, the cream was well tolerated and 94 to 100 percent of patients and investigators found its soothing effect satisfying or very satisfying. Other research is in vitro.
quick.how: It is applied as a topical cream to irritated skin, in the trial twice daily.
quick.risks: Trial tolerance was described as excellent, though pruritus and mild pain rose during radiotherapy. Sucralfate is minimally absorbed according to Wikipedia.

lead: Cicalfate+ (also written Cicalfate, from Avene) is a topical repair cream whose active ingredients are sucralfate and copper-zinc salts.[1][2]

People use it to soothe and support skin that is irritated or damaged. In a 47-patient open multicentre French study of breast radiotherapy, women applied the cream twice daily for 10 weeks; tolerance was rated excellent and soothing effect was satisfying or very satisfying in 94 to 100 percent.[1]
Sucralfate is a prescription ulcer medicine approved in the US in 1981; Wikipedia describes oral and rectal use and minimal systemic absorption.[3]

chain: Sucralfate and copper-zinc salts applied topically
Skin looks and feels more comfortable while it recovers
angle.text: The cream is used on irritated, compromised skin, for example in post-procedure or radiation-treated skin, to soothe it while it recovers.

paras: Sucralfate forms a protective paste-like barrier on tissue in acid conditions and binds proteins; Wikipedia's page covers oral and rectal use and does not describe skin use.[3]

A French open multicentre study followed 47 women with breast cancer treated with radiotherapy who applied the cream twice daily for 10 weeks. Tolerance was excellent; radiation dermatitis (NCIC score 2 or more) was seen in 5% at week 3 and 53% in the last week; pruritus increased at day 21, and pain and discomfort increased at day 28 at low intensity.[1]

A 2018 in vitro veterinary study found both Cicalfate cream and sucralfate solution inhibited several bacterial species, including Staphylococcus aureus strains and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, with differences between laboratory and clinical strains.[2]
